subject: English
topic: Sentence Completion — Advanced Vocabulary and Logic in Context (W13 B1)

questions.stem: Despite the overwhelming evidence against him, the politician remained ___, refusing to acknowledge any wrongdoing.
questions.explanation: B is correct. BRAZEN = bold and without shame; shameless in the face of wrongdoing. The sentence sets up a contrast: 'despite overwhelming evidence' (which should make someone contrite/ashamed) the politician 'refused to acknowledge' = remained shameless. BRAZEN perfectly captures defiant shamelessness. Trap: contrite = feeling remorse (the opposite of what the sentence describes); penitent = repentant (also opposite); diffident = lacking self-confidence (unrelated to shamelessness in the face of evidence).

questions.stem: The professor's lecture was so ___ that students in the back rows could not follow the complex arguments without written notes.
questions.explanation: C is correct. ABSTRUSE = difficult to understand; obscure; dealing with complex or esoteric concepts. The result clause ('students could not follow') confirms the lecture was hard to grasp — not just long, but intellectually dense. Trap: lucid = clearly expressed (the opposite — lucid would mean students could follow easily); verbose = using too many words (describes style, not comprehension difficulty — a verbose lecture could be easy to follow); eloquent = persuasive and fluent (positive quality, contradicts the difficulty implied).

questions.stem: The new CEO's management style was seen as ___ by long-term employees who were used to being consulted before any major decision was taken.
questions.explanation: B is correct. AUTOCRATIC = having or favouring absolute personal power; taking decisions without consulting others. The clue is 'used to being consulted before major decisions' — the employees expected consultation, but the new CEO did not provide it. Autocratic style = no consultation, top-down decisions. Trap: democratic = decisions made with consultation/participation (the opposite of what the employees experienced under the new CEO); laissez-faire = hands-off, letting employees decide for themselves (also opposite of the described style); transformational = inspiring change (neutral, not negative).

questions.stem: After the scandal, the company's board moved quickly to ___ the damage to its public image through a series of charitable initiatives.
questions.explanation: C is correct. MITIGATE = to make less severe or serious; to lessen the damage. The board is trying to REDUCE reputational damage through charitable acts. Mitigate = lessen, moderate. Trap: aggravate, compound, exacerbate = all mean to make worse (the opposite of what the board intends). A company doing charitable work to repair its image is mitigating the damage, not worsening it. Key: charitable initiatives are clearly remedial, not harmful.

questions.stem: The scientist's ___ observations, made over a decade of fieldwork, provided conclusive proof where earlier researchers had only found inconclusive hints.
questions.explanation: B is correct. METICULOUS = showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise. A decade of fieldwork that produced 'conclusive proof' (where others found only hints) must have involved careful, detailed observation. Meticulous perfectly captures thorough, careful scientific fieldwork. Trap: cursory = hasty and not thorough (opposite — cursory observations would not produce conclusive proof); perfunctory = done with minimal care (same problem as cursory); arbitrary = random, based on chance (contradicts systematic fieldwork).

questions.stem: The arbitrator was chosen precisely because she was ___ — she had no financial connection to either party in the dispute.
questions.explanation: A is correct. DISINTERESTED = impartial; having no personal stake in the outcome. The sentence explicitly explains she was chosen because she had 'no financial connection' to either party = she had no personal interest → she is DISINTERESTED (impartial). Trap: uninterested = not interested, bored (the arbitrator may be very interested in doing the job well; 'uninterested' implies boredom, not impartiality); indifferent = without care or concern (implies she doesn't care about the outcome, which is different from being unbiased); partisan = supporting one side (the opposite).

questions.stem: His ___ remarks at the award ceremony alienated his colleagues, who felt that his thinly veiled criticism was entirely inappropriate for the occasion.
questions.explanation: A is correct. ACERBIC = (especially of a comment or style) sharp and forthright; harsh in manner or style; biting. 'Thinly veiled criticism' = indirect but sharp attacks. ACERBIC remarks = sharp, cutting, biting words that sting. Trap: laudatory = praising (opposite — laudatory remarks at an award ceremony would be appropriate); equivocal = having more than one meaning; ambiguous (while thinly veiled might seem equivocal, the sentence says the criticism alienated people — suggesting it was understood clearly, hence more acerbic than equivocal); magnanimous = generous in spirit (opposite).

questions.stem: The expedition team's ___ approach — making decisions on the spot without any fixed schedule — proved both a strength and a liability in the unpredictable terrain.
questions.explanation: D is correct. AD HOC = improvised; done without prior planning; created for the immediate purpose. The description — 'making decisions on the spot without any fixed schedule' — is the definition of an ad hoc approach. Trap: systematic = following a plan (opposite — the team had no fixed plan); regimented = strictly organised (opposite); empirical = based on observation and evidence (neutral scientific term, not the same as unplanned improvisation). 'Ad hoc' is a Latin phrase used directly in English to mean improvised/unplanned.

questions.stem: The witness's account was filled with ___ detail — she remembered what colour curtains were in the room even though the event had occurred twenty years ago.
questions.explanation: B is correct. MINUTE (adjective, pronounced my-NYOOT) = extremely small or precise in detail; tiny and particular. 'Minute detail' = very fine, specific, granular detail. The example (remembering curtain colour after 20 years) illustrates extraordinary precision of memory. Trap: superfluous = unnecessary, excessive (different from precise detail — superfluous detail means too much irrelevant information, not precision); peripheral = relating to the outer edge, not central (describes the relevance of detail, not its fineness); fabricated = invented (suggests dishonesty, but the sentence doesn't imply the witness is lying). Note: 'MINUTE' as adjective means tiny/precise — a classic vocabulary trap since students read it as the time unit.

questions.stem: The government's attempt to ___ the unrest by offering minor concessions failed; the protesters demanded sweeping reforms, not tokenism.
questions.explanation: C is correct. PLACATE = to make (someone) less angry or upset; to appease; to conciliate. The government offered concessions to CALM the unrest (placate the protesters). 'Tokenism' in the explanation suggests small gestures intended to pacify without real change. Trap: foment = to incite or stir up (trouble/unrest) — the opposite; foment unrest would mean the government is causing more trouble (not trying to calm it); exacerbate = to make worse (also opposite); instigate = to initiate or prompt (usually used for starting trouble).
